newsitem.title: UK: UK government "outraged" by lottery salary rises.
newsitem.headline: UK government "outraged" by lottery salary rises.

text.p: The British government attacked national lottery operator Camelot Group Plc on Wednesday after the consortium announced a 40 percent rise in its executive salary bill while the sums it raised for good causes fell.

A government spokeswoman said Prime Minister Tony Blair shared the "outrage felt by the millions of Britons who buy lottery tickets" over the figures. She stressed that a reform of the national lottery was a priority for the new Labour administration.

Camelot, owned by a consortium of five British and foreign companies, said the total raised for good causes such as charities, sports and the arts dropped to 1.27 billion pounds ($2.1 billion) in the year to March from 1.42 billion pounds 12 months earlier.
Total sales of its national lottery draw tickets and instant prize scratchcards fell 10 percent to 4.7 billion pounds. The company's profit before tax declined eight percent to 70.8 million pounds.

But the total paid to Camelot directors, dubbed "fat cats" by their critics in the British press, soared to 2.35 million pounds from 1.67 million in the previous year. Chief executive Tim Holley saw his pay package increase by 53 percent to 590,000 pounds.
To add to the company's embarrassment, Camelot was forced to release the results several days early after they were leaked to a trade magazine.
The government repeated its intention to hand the lottery over to a non-profit making organisation when Camelot's seven-year licence expires in 2001.
"It is the people's money and I am determined that it should work in their interests," Chris Smith, the minister responsible for arts and culture said in a statement.
Smith is demanding an urgent meeting with Camelot chairman Sir George Russell to discuss the company's actions and how public support for the lottery can be maintained.

He promised legislation later this year to reform the lottery. Labour has said it wants to use income from a second midweek draw introduced in February to create a one billion pound fund for health and education projects.
Launched in November 1994, the lottery is played regularly by some 30 million Britons who dream of getting rich quick with jackpots that can top 10 million pounds.
But its critics have slammed it as "a tax on the poor" while churchmen have expressed concern that it is encouraging gambling.
A Camelot spokesman said the steep rise in executive salaries was because of the part payment of long-term bonuses earned for the successful lottery launch and its first three years of operation.
The drop in sales was caused by a sharp decline in sales of scratchcards in the second year after their introduction.

"We are, however, ahead of our targets and, as long as there are no further significant changes in the gaming market which would adversely affect the lottery, we remain confident of hitting the nine billion pound target for good causes over the licence period," chairman Sir George Russell said in a statement.
Camelot, owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, De La Rue Plc, GTECH UK, Racal Electronics and ICL notes its profit after tax remains less than one penny in the pound.($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
